Screened Electrification Equipment — the selection book#

The same rules-based grid-supplier portfolio, now holding only the half of it that the evidence favours. Every name is still selected by rule from SEC filings; the new step ranks them by two facts in their own accounts and keeps the better half.

Window: January 2019 – August 2026 · The grid-tight period (January 2023 on) is reported separately throughout · Trading costs in Costs · Management fee not assumed

The idea in one paragraph#

Electricity demand is growing faster than the grid can carry it, and someone is being paid to build the difference. Our published book owns the suppliers being paid — equipment makers and electrical contractors that spend about 2 cents of each revenue dollar on physical assets, against a utility's 44 — and it deliberately did not try to pick winners among them: every qualifying name got equal money. This proposal drops that last restraint. Since the grid became genuinely tight in 2023, two facts in a supplier's own filings have separated the winners from the rest, and we now use them to hold only the stronger half.

What changes, and what does not#

Rules 1–5 of the published book are unchanged: suppliers not owners of the grid (low capital intensity), a company that says so in its own 10-K, profitable on the numbers known at the time, not dependent on subsidies, and liquid. Rules 7–9 — the risk overlay — are unchanged too.

Rule 6 is replaced. The published book held every qualifying name equally because we had no evidence we could rank them. We now do.

6. We hold the half of the list that scores best on two facts from the accounts.

  • How little the company spends on capital, relative to its sales. Within an already capital-light list, the lightest keep doing better: they convert the buildout into cash now rather than into assets that earn later.
  • Whether its revenue growth is speeding up. This year's growth rate minus last year's, on trailing-twelve-month revenue as filed. A supplier whose orders are accelerating is the one the buildout is reaching.

Each fact is ranked across the whole ~146-name eligible universe each month, the two ranks are averaged, and at each rebalance we hold the top half of the qualifying names, equally weighted. Both inputs are read from filings as published on the day — no restated numbers, no hindsight. The book holds 17 names today (14 on average since 2023), against 35 for the published book.

Why these two and not others. We tested fourteen candidate stock-ranking signals over the same universe — earnings surprises, revenue surprises, momentum, reversal, and the stocks' sensitivity to wholesale power prices, grid congestion and scarcity pricing. These were the only two with a consistent relationship to future returns, and the power-market signals — which sound the most relevant — ranked stocks no better than chance. We also tried adding links to related firms (10-K text similarity, shared headquarters city): none improved the result.

How we control risk#

Unchanged from the published book: 7. position size scaled to 20% target volatility; 8. size cut again when the book is extended far above its trend or the market; 9. 15% held in gold and Treasuries. The concentrated book needs these more, not less:

stage Sharpe return a year worst drawdown
Selected names, no risk control 1.00 33.6% −47.3%
+ volatility target 1.05 27.5% −28.8%
+ valuation de-lever 1.04 25.2% −28.8%
+ gold/Treasury sleeve (the book) 1.08 23.1% −24.1%

No look-ahead#

Every decision in the backtest uses only information that existed on the day it was made:

  • Which companies qualify — SIC codes as filed, 10-K wording only from filings published before the year being decided, earnings and capital spending as first reported (never restated), liquidity over the trailing year, and a name trades only after a year of price history.
  • The ranking — each month-end score uses filings filed by that date; a rebalance uses the latest month-end score on or before the rebalance day.
  • The risk overlay — position size is set from volatility up to yesterday; the valuation cut is set from the previous month's reading.
  • The hedge — sized from the trailing year of returns ending yesterday, with 2018 as the first trailing year (no back-filling).

What the backtest cannot remove is research hindsight: the two-factor ranking was chosen in September 2026 after testing fourteen candidates on this same history. The rules use no future data, but the choice of rules was made knowing how 2019–2026 turned out. That is addressed in Risks and by the live record kept from August 2026.

Drawdowns and market sensitivity#

The book carries 0.60 beta to the S&P 500 over the full period (0.74 since 2023) against 1.07 for GRID, and captures 78% of the market's up days against 69% of its down days.

Is this alpha?#

In fairness: yes against the grid-equipment index, in the regime it is built for — and most of that alpha was already in the published book. The selection step adds a smaller, less certain piece on top.

The test is a regression of the book's daily return on GRID's: whatever return is left over after accounting for the book's exposure to the theme is alpha. A t-statistic above 2 means the result is unlikely to be luck. This regression is a measurement made after the fact over each window; the strategy itself never uses it — the tradable, look-ahead-free version of "the book minus the theme" is the hedged book below.

alpha a year (t-statistic) full period 2019–22 2022 on 2023 on
Selection book vs GRID 9.8% (2.4) 1.9% (0.3) 14.6% (3.1) 17.5% (3.2)
Published book vs GRID 8.8% (2.3) 2.4% (0.5) 11.8% (2.7) 14.7% (2.8)
Selection book vs published book — the selection itself 1.5% (0.8) −0.4% (−0.1) 3.4% (1.7) 3.9% (1.6)
Selection book vs S&P 500 11.4% (2.7) 5.5% (0.9) 14.7% (2.8) 15.7% (2.5)

Three honest readings:

  1. Against GRID the alpha is real and statistically strong since 2022–23 (t above 3), and it is positive — though small — even in 2019–22. By the test we set for ourselves before starting this work (positive in both halves, t at least 1.5 over the whole period), it qualifies.
  2. Most of it is not new. The published book already beat GRID by 14.7% a year since 2023. That alpha comes from how the book is built — capital-light suppliers, the volatility target, the hedge sleeve — not from ranking names.
  3. The selection adds about 4 points a year since 2023, at t ≈ 1.6 — suggestive, not proven, and zero before 2022. It also carries a hindsight caveat: the two-factor score was chosen in September 2026 after testing fourteen candidates. We froze it on 24 September 2026 and record its picks every month from August 2026; that live record is the real test.

The hedged version: owning the alpha without the theme#

For an investor who already owns the theme, or wants the stock selection without the sector's swings, the book can be run short an index ETF against it. The hedge size on each day is the book's beta to the ETF over the preceding 252 trading days — for the first days of 2019 that year is 2018, from the identical screening rule run over 2018, so nothing is filled in from the future. (Corrected 25 September 2026: an earlier version left the 2018 book empty, so every hedge started 2019 near zero and was under-sized all year. The fix changes nothing from 2022 on; the full-period and 2019–22 hedged figures below are lower than first published, because 2019 is now actually hedged — see the correction note.) Choosing the hedge#

The fair way to pick a hedge is by how closely it tracks the book — something an investor can measure before knowing the results — not by which one produced the best hedged return afterwards.

hedge correlation with the book, 2018–22 risk left after hedging, 2018–22 correlation, 2023 on risk left, 2023 on
GRID 0.73 11.9% 0.78 10.1%
PAVE 0.77 11.0% 0.84 8.7%
XLI 0.76 11.3% 0.77 10.2%
½ GRID + ½ PAVE 0.78 10.9% 0.85 8.5%
⅓ GRID + ⅓ PAVE + ⅓ XLI 0.78 10.8% 0.84 8.7%

PAVE is offered as a hedge on these grounds. It tracked the book more closely than GRID already in 2018–22, before the period the strategy is judged on, so choosing it is not hindsight. The reason is composition: PAVE holds only US-listed infrastructure and industrial companies — contractors, electrical equipment, machinery — which is what this book owns. GRID is global and includes electric utilities, which the book excludes by rule, so shorting it adds exposure to utilities, European stocks and currencies that the book does not have.

The blends track the book best of all (0.78 in 2018–22; the 50/50 GRID and PAVE blend 0.85 since 2023) and spread the hedge across funds, but the 50/50 blend's hedged return since 2023 (Sharpe 1.31, Calmar 2.10) sits between the two it is made of. PAVE alone has the best hedged figures (1.40 / 2.91). We offer GRID, PAVE and the 50/50 blend, and would recommend PAVE or the 50/50 blend for an investor choosing today.

Can you short these? Yes. GRID is an $11.8bn fund trading about $100m a day and PAVE a $13.5bn fund trading about $82m a day, both with listed options; XLI ($32bn, $1.3bn a day) is the most liquid of the three. Large ETFs are normally cheap to borrow, but we have not verified these rates, which is why we charge 0.5% a year. An institutional investor would more often use a total-return swap on the index than a physical short.

Hedged Sharpes use the same 4% risk-free rate and are not credited with interest on the short proceeds, which understates them slightly.

A single-name short option#

Instead of an index ETF, the hedge can short the weakest names in the same eligible universe: each month, the bottom fifth of the ~146 eligible electrification names by a 14-signal score (method below). These are capital-heavy, slowing-revenue, weak-momentum names that sell off with the theme but have lagged it: the basket shorted here rose 12.4% a year over the full period, against 20.8% for PAVE and 23.1% for the book.

It is shown two ways: sized like the ETF hedges (the book's trailing 252-day beta to the basket, no look-ahead), and as a fixed $0.25 short per $1 of book. Single names are charged 1% a year to borrow (the ETFs 0.5%), 10bp on the basket's monthly re-formation and 10bp on every change in hedge size.

What the tables say.

  • Since 2023 the single-name short is the strongest hedge. Fully hedged it keeps 24.4% a year against 17.1% for PAVE, at a higher Sharpe (1.59 vs 1.40) and Calmar (3.64 vs 2.91).
  • Over the whole period it is at least level, with a deeper drawdown. Fully hedged it has the highest full-period Sharpe (0.92 vs XLI 0.74, PAVE 0.70) and 2019–22 Sharpe (0.36 vs 0.33 / 0.20), but XLI and PAVE have smaller worst drawdowns (−11% / −12% vs −17%); full-period Calmar is XLI 1.06, PAVE 0.92, single names 0.91.
  • It is not the better tracker. By the ex-ante criterion used above, it tracks the book less closely than PAVE: correlation 0.66 in 2018–22 and 0.70 since 2023 (PAVE 0.77 / 0.84). Its edge is not closer tracking but a cheaper short. It is a second stock-selection bet, on the losers.
  • At $0.25 per $1 the choice matters little. Every hedge costs Sharpe in 2019–22 and adds a little since 2023. The single-name short matches PAVE on Sharpe since 2023 (1.80) with a higher Calmar (2.72 vs 2.35), and is about level with XLI over the full period.

Recommendation: PAVE stays the default hedge, chosen without hindsight and traded in one line. The single-name short is an alternative for an investor who wants to keep more of the return and can borrow single names. Treat its extra return as a second selection bet with the same caveats as the long side.

Correction: 2019 hedge sizing#

Every trailing-beta hedge on this page sizes its short from the book's beta over the preceding year. The first published version computed the 2019 ratios from an empty 2018 book — the screen's membership had only been built from January 2019 — so each hedge started near zero and reached its normal size only late in 2019. The screen has now been run over 2018 with the identical rule (it reproduces the published 2019–26 membership in every month) and the hedges re-sized from that.

Nothing from 2022 on changes — those ratios only look back to 2021. The unhedged book and the fixed $0.25 hedges do not change at all. What changes is 2019–22, because hedging the book's best year (+53% in 2019) properly costs return:

How the single-name short is computed#

  1. Universe. The same mechanically eligible electrification universe the long book is drawn from (SIC electrical-equipment / power codes plus the fuel-cycle vocabulary, $10m a day liquidity): about 146 names a month, 29 held short on average (40 today).
  2. Score. At each month-end, 14 signals are computed from information available that day: - filings as first reported: capital spending relative to sales, revenue acceleration, revenue growth, revenue and earnings surprises, asset growth; - prices: 12-month momentum, 1-month reversal; - wholesale power markets: each stock's trailing beta to PJM/ERCOT energy prices, PJM congestion and ERCOT scarcity pricing, and each beta times the last three months' move in that price.

Each signal is trimmed at the 5th/95th percentile, standardised across that month's universe, and the 14 are averaged with equal weight, with no fitting and no sign chosen from results. 3. Basket. The bottom fifth by that score is bought equally weighted on the next trading day and held, weights drifting, until the next month-end, when it is re-formed. Turnover is high (about 11× the basket per year), costing about 1.1% a year per $1 shorted at 10bp. 4. Sizing. - Beta-sized: each day's short is the book's beta to the basket over the preceding 252 trading days, lagged one day and capped at 2, exactly as for the ETFs. - Fixed: $0.25 per $1 of book, every day. 5. Costs. 1% a year borrow on the short notional; 10bp on basket turnover and on each change in hedge size. Short proceeds earn no interest (understates the hedged Sharpe slightly).

What is and is not look-ahead-free.

  • No look-ahead: the score, the basket and both sizings use only data available on the day.
  • Hindsight: the 14-signal score was assembled in September 2026 after seeing how each of its parts ranked stocks, the same caveat as the long side's two-factor score.
  • Not checked: single-name borrow availability and cost. The thinnest names trade about $10m a day, which limits how large a fund can run this short.
  • The 2018 warm-up is a real book. The trailing year behind the first 2019 hedge ratios is the same screening rule run over 2018 (it reproduces the published 2019–26 membership exactly). One data limit: EDGAR full-text hits start in January 2017, so the 2018 book sees one year of 10-K wording rather than the four the rule asks for (the published 2019 book sees two).

Risks#

The selection was chosen with hindsight. The two-factor score was picked in September 2026 after fourteen candidates were tested on this same history, and "hold the top half" was one of several ways of using it. The backtest therefore flatters it. The score has been frozen since 24 September 2026 and its picks are logged every month; until that live record exists, treat the selection's extra 4 points a year as an estimate, not a track record.

It only works once the grid is tight. In 2019–22 the selection added nothing (−0.4% a year against the published book) and cost 2020 dearly. If the buildout slows and capital intensity and revenue acceleration stop distinguishing suppliers, the book reverts to a more concentrated — and therefore riskier — version of the published one.

It is concentrated, and was very concentrated early. 17 names today and 14 on average since 2023, but only 3–4 in 2019 and as few as one at a rebalance. The early figures, good and bad, rest on a handful of stocks. The full-period drawdown (−24.1% against −20.0%) is the cost of that concentration.

The hedge is an estimate. Hedge size comes from a trailing beta that can lag a regime change, and the borrow cost is assumed, not observed.

We still have no exit signal. Nothing here tells us when the buildout ends; the overlay limits what a downturn costs, it does not predict one.
